content: The data from various studies on the treatment of uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria in endemic settings, primarily in Africa, provides insights into the efficacy and safety of different antimalarial regimens. Below is a detailed summary of the findings: 1. Early Vomiting: Based on data from 2,695 participants across three randomized controlled trials, the incidence of early vomiting was 20 per 1,000 participants. The difference observed was an increase of 10 cases per 1,000 participants, with moderate certainty due to a serious risk of bias. 2. Vomiting: Data from 6,761 participants in nine randomized controlled trials showed a vomiting rate of 90 per 1,000 participants. No difference was observed between the intervention and comparator groups. The evidence was rated as moderate due to a serious risk of bias. 3. Nausea: The incidence of nausea was reported as 20 per 1,000 participants, based on data from 4,531 participants in nine studies. A reduction of six cases per 1,000 participants was observed, with moderate certainty due to a serious risk of bias. 4. Diarrhea: Among 4,889 participants in seven studies, the incidence of diarrhea was 120 per 1,000 participants, with no difference between groups. The evidence was rated as moderate due to a serious risk of bias. 5. Abdominal Pain: Data from 911 participants in five studies showed an incidence of 190 per 1,000 participants, with a reduction of 30 cases per 1,000 participants. The evidence was rated as low due to serious risks of bias and imprecision. 6. Anorexia: Among 3,834 participants in five studies, the incidence of anorexia was 150 per 1,000 participants, with a reduction of 10 cases per 1,000 participants. The evidence was rated as moderate due to a serious risk of bias. 7. Headache: Data from 309 participants in two studies showed an incidence of 270 per 1,000 participants, with an increase of 60 cases per 1,000 participants. The evidence was rated as low due to serious risks of bias and imprecision. 8. Sleeplessness: Among 547 participants in two studies, the incidence of sleeplessness was 10 per 1,000 participants, with an increase of 20 cases per 1,000 participants. The evidence was rated as low due to serious risks of bias and imprecision. 9. Dizziness: Data from 547 participants in two studies showed an incidence of 30 per 1,000 participants, with an increase of 10 cases per 1,000 participants. The evidence was rated as low due to serious risks of bias and imprecision. 10. Sleepiness: Among 384 participants in one study, no cases of sleepiness were reported. The evidence was rated as low due to serious risks of bias and imprecision. 11. Weakness: Data from 1,812 participants in five studies showed an incidence of 170 per 1,000 participants, with an increase of 10 cases per 1,000 participants. The evidence was rated as moderate due to a serious risk of bias. 12. Cough: Among 4,342 participants in five studies, the incidence of cough was 420 per 1,000 participants, with no difference between groups. The evidence was rated as moderate due to a serious risk of bias. 13. Coryza: Data from 832 participants in two studies showed an incidence of 680 per 1,000 participants, with a reduction of 20 cases per 1,000 participants. The evidence was rated as low due to serious imprecision. 14. Prolonged QT Interval (Adverse Event): Among 1,548 participants in one study, the incidence of prolonged QT interval was 30 per 1,000 participants, with a reduction of 10 cases per 1,000 participants. The evidence was rated as low due to serious imprecision and bias. 15. Prolonged QT Interval (Bazett Correction): Data from 1,548 participants in one study showed an incidence of 70 per 1,000 participants, with an increase of 20 cases per 1,000 participants. The evidence was rated as low due to serious imprecision and bias. 16. Prolonged QT Interval (Fridericia Correction): Among 1,548 participants in one study, no cases of prolonged QT interval were reported. The evidence was rated as low due to serious risks of bias and imprecision. 17. Pruritus: Data from 2,033 participants in five studies showed an incidence of 20 per 1,000 participants, with an increase of 20 cases per 1,000 participants. The evidence was rated as moderate due to a serious risk of bias. 18. Facial Edema: Among 384 participants in one study, the findings were consistent across trials, but the evidence was rated as low due to serious imprecision and bias. 19. Serious Adverse Events (Including Deaths): Data from 3,522 participants in eight studies showed an incidence of eight per 1,000 participants, with an increase of one case per 1,000 participants. The evidence was rated as moderate due to serious imprecision. 20. Treatment Failure on Day 28 (PCR-Unadjusted): Based on data from 143 participants in one study, no treatment failures were reported. The evidence was rated as very low due to serious indirectness and imprecision. 21. Treatment Failure on Day 28 (PCR-Adjusted): Similarly, no treatment failures were reported in the same study. The evidence was rated as very low due to serious indirectness and imprecision. 22. Fever Clearance on Day 2: Among 144 participants in one study, no participants in either group had fever on day 2. The evidence was rated as very low due to serious indirectness and imprecision. 23. Arthralgia: Data from 1,148 participants in one study showed an incidence of six per 1,000 participants, with a reduction of one case per 1,000 participants. The evidence was rated as moderate due to a serious risk of bias. 24. Myalgia: Among 1,148 participants in one study, the incidence of myalgia was six per 1,000 participants, with no difference between groups. The evidence was rated as moderate due to a serious risk of bias. 25. Urticaria: Data from 719 participants in two studies showed an incidence of two per 1,000 participants, with a reduction of one case per 1,000 participants. The evidence was rated as low due to serious risks of bias and imprecision. 26. Rash: Among 220 participants in one study, the findings were consistent across trials, but the evidence was rated as low due to serious imprecision and bias. Overall, the studies highlight the need for further research to address limitations such as bias, imprecision, and indirectness. Many trials were underpowered, and additional studies in diverse settings are required to generalize the findings.
